title: The poets of Anandpur
hook: tradition says he kept dozens of poets at his court

segments.voice: Yesterday, languages of the court: Persian for the emperor, Punjabi for the people, Braj for poetry. Your line was many tongues. Who did you greet in theirs? Day one thousand two hundred forty-one.

Anandpur, in the hills. A town under threat for years, drilling soldiers, storing grain, watching the passes. And in the middle of it, tradition says, a room full of poets. Dozens of them, gathered by Guru Gobind Singh, writing, translating, reciting. A fort that keeps poets is a strange sight. Under pressure, the extras usually get cut first. The Guru, by this memory, did the opposite. Today is about that court, and about one poet whose words are still sung.
screen: `A TOWN UNDER THREAT.` → `A ROOM FULL OF POETS.` → `THE OPPOSITE OF CUTTING EXTRAS.`

segments.voice: Sikh tradition remembers the poets of Anandpur as a gathering of writers from different backgrounds: Sikhs and others, scholars of Sanskrit and of Persian. Tradition says the Guru set them to work bringing older works of story and wisdom into Braj, so that ordinary people could reach what had been locked in learned languages. The idea was to open the books, not to guard them. Tradition also tells of a great collection of this work, sometimes called Vidya Sagar, the ocean of learning, and says much of it was lost in the flooded Sarsa river when Anandpur was left. Nobody now can read what went under. One poet's work did survive, and Sikhs still sing it. Bhai Nand Lal, called Goya, wrote in Persian, ghazals and couplets of love for the Guru. Paraphrased, he writes of the Guru's face as the thing he longs to see, and of a single glance from the Guru being worth more than the world. Sikh practice gives his poems a place in kirtan, alongside the Gurus' own hymns. Why would a Guru at war keep a court of poets? Some readers answer: because what he was defending was not only land. It was a way of life, and a way of life needs songs, stories and learning to carry it. Swords protect a people; poems tell them who they are. The court of poets was the second half of the defense.
screen: `A GATHERING OF WRITERS.` · `OPENING THE BOOKS, NOT GUARDING THEM.` · `LOST IN THE SARSA, TRADITION SAYS.` · `BHAI NAND LAL, STILL SUNG.` · then, large: `A COURT OF POETS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a poem aloud. Pick any short poem: a hymn, a verse you learned as a kid, a few lines you love, a song lyric you know by heart. Read it, or say it, out loud, slowly, once. Listen to your own voice carrying it. Then sit quietly and let the last line keep sounding in you. Notice which word stays. If you pray, you can let the poem lead you into Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
The poets of Anandpur. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh kept dozens of poets at his court, translating and writing; Bhai Nand Lal's Persian poems are still sung. Today's word.
Your line: a court of poets. Today, send the poem you read to one person, with a line about why it stayed with you. Day one thousand two hundred forty-one.

notes: 'Dozens of poets' follows the index ('tradition says he kept dozens'); some accounts give a specific number (often fifty-two). The number is deliberately left out; please decide whether to add it as tradition.
The translation work into Braj, the collection called Vidya Sagar and its loss in the Sarsa during the evacuation of Anandpur are all given as tradition; please confirm.
Bhai Nand Lal's lines are paraphrased loosely (the Guru's face, a glance worth more than the world); please check against the Diwan-i-Goya or Zindagi Nama.
'Something Sikh practice allows for very few writers beyond the Gurus' refers to the Rehat Maryada permitting kirtan of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal alongside Gurbani; please confirm the wording.
Tomorrow is the rehatnamas, some of which are attributed to Bhai Nand Lal; deliberately not mentioned today.
